title: Rav Asi
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: This is the name by which he is usually called in the Babylonian Talmud; only occasionally have copyists corrupted it to “Rabbi Asi.” In the Jerusalem Talmud he is usually called simply Asi, like the other Babylonian amoraim who did not receive ordination and were called only by their names, such as Abba, Shmuel’s father; Shmuel; Kahana; Zeiri; and others.

We have found no information anywhere about his parents or family, nor do we know who his teachers were. We do know, however, that he was the head of the community in Huzal. Thus, Megillah 5b reports that Rav Asi read the Megillah in Huzal on both the fourteenth and fifteenth, since it was a city surrounded by a wall from the days of Yehoshua ben Nun. (Sefer Yuchasin writes that Huzal was near Nehardea.)
Chullin 26b likewise states: “Rav Asi instituted in Huzal.” The same reading is required there at 107a: the text mistakenly has Rav Ashi, but should read Rav Asi.

When Rav came to Nehardea, he found Rav Asi and his colleague Rav Kahana already among the leading sages of the generation. According to the testimony of the geonim quoted in Zikhron la-Rishonim, §274: “Rav, Rav Asi, and Shmuel were almost equal in standing.” This is indeed borne out explicitly in Bava Kamma 80b: Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Asi came to a celebration marking a son’s birth. Rav would not enter before Shmuel, and Shmuel would not enter before Rav Asi. Rashi explains that Rav Asi was greater than Shmuel.

Sanhedrin 36b states that Rav Kahana and Rav Asi needed Rav’s received traditions, but did not need his reasoning. Rav had spent most of his life in the Land of Israel, in the academy of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, and had received from them all the explanations of the Mishnah. They therefore needed his received traditions—the authentic readings and explanations—but did not need his reasoning. This accords with what we have said: when Rav came to Babylonia, he already found them among the generation’s leading sages. Shabbat 146b states that Rav would not sit on a cushioned seat out of respect for “our teachers,” meaning Rav Kahana and Rav Asi. Megillah 5b, Kiddushin 44b, and Sanhedrin 29b report that an incident occurred and Rav took Rav Asi’s opinion into account. In Sukkah 6b and Beitzah 10a and 37b, Rav Kahana and Rav Asi spoke to Rav, and Rav remained silent. In Pesachim 106b, Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba visited Rav Asi, who said, “Leave him alone; he holds like his teacher”—meaning Rav. From this we see explicitly that Rav was not Rav Asi’s teacher. In Ketubot 89b they addressed Rav, “According to you”; in Nazir 19a they said to him, “Why did you not explain it to us?” Their disagreements appear in Megillah 5a, Kiddushin 45b, Gittin 25a, Sanhedrin 29b, and Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 1:1, Gittin 3:1, and Bava Kamma 10:3.
When Rav traveled to towns to judge cases and issue rulings, Rav Kahana and Rav Asi accompanied him, as in Avodah Zarah 57a and Chullin 95b.

They knew how to honor Rav and recognized his eminence as truly the foremost sage of the entire Diaspora. Thus, in Chullin 44b they said to him, “You have taught us, our teacher.” In Bava Batra 51a they said, “Has the Master retracted his teaching?” In Pesachim 113a Rav told Rav Asi, “Do not live in a town where no horse neighs,” and so forth.
We also find “Rav Asi said in Rav’s name” in Shabbat 22a, Beitzah 16a, Sotah 30a, and Avodah Zarah 38a.

Nevertheless, Rav Asi had an academy of his own, with students gathered around him, even where Rav was present. This is evident from Jerusalem Talmud 1:7: Rav instructed his students, “Do not sit on the outside table of Asi’s study hall, for it is cold.”
Similarly, Ketubot 48b, Kiddushin 46a, and Keritot 17a relate: “Chiyya bar Rav raised an objection to Rav Asi; Rav said to them,” and so forth.

Besides Rav, who was greater than he, we find Levi, whom Rav Asi called “my teacher,” in Avodah Zarah 38b. Shmuel, however, was entirely his peer; Bava Kamma 80b even implies that Rav Asi was greater than Shmuel. Yevamot 41a likewise states: “Shmuel and Rav Asi both said.” Their disagreements appear in Jerusalem Talmud Kiddushin 3:7 and Niddah 1:3.

Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba, who was a disciple-colleague of Rav, was also like a colleague to him, as in Pesachim 106b. His colleague Rav Kahana went up to the Land of Israel and remained there; consequently, we do not find many rulings exchanged between the two. Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 3:3 nevertheless records Rabbi Idi saying, “Kahana and Asi disagreed.”

We also find Binyamin Ganzakhaya disagreeing with Rav Asi in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:6. Apart from these sages, all Rav’s students—even the greatest of them, such as Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah—received teachings from Rav Asi. Thus, Rav Huna reports in Rav Asi’s name in Bava Batra 126a and Chullin 19a. In Ketubot 48b he objected to Rav Asi, who replied, “Did I not tell you not to follow the opposite position?” Tosafot on Berakhot 34b also write to this effect.

Rav Yehudah likewise reports in Rav Asi’s name in Shabbat 22a; Yevamot 16b; Ketubot 77a and 105a; Nedarim 21b; Gittin 57a and 64b; Kiddushin 11a and 81b; Shevuot 41b; and Jerusalem Talmud Shekalim 6:3.

Yevamot 17a has Rav Yehudah reporting in Rav Asi’s name and then saying, “When I said it before Shmuel,” and so forth. Rashi explains that after Rav Asi’s death Rav Yehudah went to study before Shmuel. This is indeed so: although Shmuel maintained his distinguished academy in Nehardea, after Rav’s death they all went before Rav Asi. Since Rav Asi did not live long after Rav, however, as we shall explain below, the Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon, part 3, chapter 2, says that after Rav died Shmuel became head of the academy.
We likewise find that Rav’s other students received teachings from Rav Asi.
Rabbi Abba reports in Rav Asi’s name in Bava Batra 140b; in Ketubot 43a the text mistakenly has Rabbi Yose.
Rav Ada bar Rav Aza reports in Rav Asi’s name in Kiddushin 81b; Geniva does so in Chullin 56b; and Daniel bar Rav Katina does so at the beginning of Shabbat, chapter 3.
Rav Hamnuna reports in Asi’s name in Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 3:1. Chiyya bar Ashi reports in his name in Jerusalem Talmud Gittin 9:9 and Kiddushin 3:8.

Rav Chisda reports in Ashi’s name—where the reading should be Asi—at the beginning of Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat, chapter 1, at 20b, again at the end of halakhah 1, and in 11:2. Mevo ha-Yerushalmi conjectures that this Ashi was the father of Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi. This is an error, for the reading must undoubtedly be “Asi.”
Rav Amram reports in his name in Eruvin 102a; Rami bar Abba reports in Rav Asi’s name in Eruvin 100b; and Rami bar Chama does so there as well.

Rav Sheshet reports in Rav Asi’s name in Sanhedrin 33a and Chullin 92b. Of his private life we know only that he was wealthy and owned property. Chullin 105a relates that he inspected his property every day, saying, “Where are all those coins of Master Shmuel?” One day he saw a channel bursting into his land. He took his cloak, rolled it up, and placed it in the opening. He called out, people came and stopped the breach, and he said, “I have found all Master Shmuel’s coins.”

We also find that he took care with the cup of blessing: he spread a cloth over his head and took the cup in both hands, as in Berakhot 51a. The circumstances of his death are related in Niddah 36b. Rav held that a woman experiencing the relevant bleeding was a niddah for that day. Before his death Rav instructed Rav Asi to tell his student Sheila bar Avina to retract his ruling, and, if he refused, “garyei”—draw him back with convincing arguments. Rav Asi thought Rav had said “gadyei,” meaning to cut him off by excommunication. After Rav died, Rav Asi told Sheila, “Retract, for Rav retracted.” Sheila replied, “Had he retracted, he would have told me himself.” He did not obey Rav Asi, who excommunicated him. Sheila said, “Is the Master not afraid of being burned?”—that is, perhaps you will be scorched by my coal. Rav Asi answered, “I am Isi ben Yehudah ben Gur Aryeh—a copper mortar over which decay has no power.” Sheila replied, “And I am Sheila bar Avina—an iron pestle that breaks a copper mortar.” Rav Asi became ill; they brought him into warmth and took him out of cold, and Rav Asi died. Sheila bar Avina died afterward. From this we see that Rav Asi died almost immediately after Rav. The death of Rav Asi mentioned in Kiddushin 13a, however, refers to Rabbi Asi, the colleague of Rabbi Ami, as is evident there.

notes.text: The passage quoted without a tractate name is Jerusalem Talmud Beitzah 1:7. Its “outside table” refers to seating in Asi’s study hall.
Hyman argues that Rav was not Rav Asi’s teacher, although Asi received traditions from him. Rashi on Bava Kamma 80b explicitly calls Rav Asi a pupil of Rav.
The Sanhedrin 36b quotation prints “Rav Adi” in the supplied Hebrew; the Talmudic passage reads “Rav Asi.”
The account of Sheila bar Avina continues into Niddah 37a. Hyman abridges the list of names in Rav Asi’s reply; it is part of the story’s play on names, not a statement of Rav Asi’s genealogy.

Compare Hyman’s separate articles on [Rabbi Asi, colleague of Rabbi Ami](https://www.girsology.com/toledot?entry=h-63bc6d04b074b84e&lang=en) and [Rav Athi (Ithi), colleague of Rav Ashi](https://www.girsology.com/toledot?entry=h-d5d9554b20b20d28&lang=en).
